notes.meaning: The people of Israel turned away from God again and fell back into worshiping idols. Because of their disobedience, God allowed their neighbors, the Philistines, to conquer and rule over them for forty years. Unlike earlier times in the book of Judges, the Israelites did not even cry out to God for help, showing how hardened their hearts had become.

A man named Manoah lived in the town of Zorah, near the Philistine border, and belonged to the tribe of Dan. His wife was barren and had never been able to bear any children. Throughout the Bible, God often gave important leaders to mothers who had waited a long time for a child.

The angel of the Lord appeared to Manoah's wife while she was alone. He told her he knew she had no children, but promised she would soon conceive and give birth to a son. Many Christian teachers understand this divine messenger to be a special appearance of God the Son before He was born in Bethlehem as Jesus.

The angel instructed the woman not to drink any wine or strong alcohol, and not to eat any food considered unclean by God's law. Because the unborn baby was being dedicated to God, the food and drink taken by the mother would directly affect him. Her careful obedience was required so the child would be set apart for God from the very start.

The angel said the boy's hair must never be cut with a razor because he would be a Nazirite dedicated to God from before his birth. A Nazirite was someone who took a special vow of holy separation to the Lord, though Samson's vow was given by God for his whole life. The angel also revealed that this boy would begin the rescue of Israel from Philistine control, though full victory would come later under King David.

The woman went directly to her husband and told him that a man of God had spoken to her. She described the visitor as having a face so bright and awesome that he looked like an angel. She explained that she felt so much awe that she did not dare ask his name or where he came from.

She repeated the messenger's instructions to Manoah, explaining that she was forbidden from drinking wine, strong liquor, or eating unclean food. She emphasized that the child would belong to God as a Nazirite for his entire life, until the day he died. Sharing what God had said allowed both husband and wife to support each other in following God's commands.

Manoah believed what his wife told him and prayed earnestly to the Lord. He asked God to send the man of God back to them so they could learn how to raise and train the promised boy properly. God is pleased when parents ask for His guidance in raising their children.

God heard Manoah's prayer and sent the angel back to the woman while she was sitting in the field. Manoah was not present at that moment, but the angel waited for him to be called. God kindly meets those who genuinely want to learn their duty.

The woman ran in a hurry to find her husband and tell him the good news. She announced that the very same visitor who had spoken to her before had appeared again. She wanted Manoah to meet the messenger and hear the instructions himself.

Manoah quickly got up and followed his wife into the field to meet the visitor. When he reached the man, he asked if he was the one who had spoken to his wife earlier, and the angel confirmed that he was. Manoah's quick response showed his eagerness to hear God's word.

Manoah declared his faith by expressing confidence that the angel's words would certainly come true. He then asked what standard of life the boy should follow and what work he was appointed to do. He wanted to know how to manage the child so they would not fail in their duty.

The angel of the Lord replied by pointing back to the rules he had already given to Manoah's wife. He did not tell Manoah about the future deeds of the boy, but kept the focus on obedience. God expects His people to focus on doing their present duty rather than guessing the future.

The angel repeated the commands with greater detail, stating that the woman must not eat anything produced by the grapevine, including grapes and raisins. She was strictly warned against drinking wine or strong drink, and told never to touch anything unclean. God called both parents to practice careful self-control to protect the holy calling of their child.

Manoah politely urged the visitor to remain with them so they could prepare a young goat for him to eat. He assumed the visitor was an ordinary human prophet and wanted to treat him with hospitality. In the ancient world, offering a meal was the common way to honor a distinguished guest.

The angel told Manoah that even if he stayed, he would not eat ordinary food. He instructed Manoah instead to offer the goat as a burnt offering to the Lord if he wanted to make a gift. Manoah did not realize that the person speaking to him was an angel sent directly from heaven.

Manoah asked the angel for his name so that they could honor him when the promise came to pass. He likely wanted to send him gifts or give public credit to his message once the baby was born. Manoah wanted to show proper respect to the messenger God had sent.

The angel replied by asking why Manoah asked for his name, explaining that his name is wonderful and beyond human understanding. This word points to the greatness and mystery of God, whose full nature cannot be grasped by human beings. Many commentators connect this word with the title 'Wonderful' used for the Messiah in the book of Isaiah.

Manoah placed the young goat and a grain offering upon a large rock to present them to the Lord. While Manoah and his wife stood watching, the Lord performed an astonishing miracle before their eyes. Fire came forth to consume the offering on the rock, showing that God had accepted their worship.

As the sacrificial fire rose from the rock toward the sky, the angel of the Lord stepped into the flame and ascended heavenward. When Manoah and his wife saw this terrifying and glorious sight, they fell facedown on the ground in worship. The miracle proved that their visitor was truly divine and had returned to heaven.

The angel disappeared from their sight and did not return to visit them again. It was at this moment that Manoah finally realized the visitor was the angel of the Lord Himself. The supernatural sign confirmed everything the messenger had promised.

Overcome with fear, Manoah told his wife that they were doomed to die because they had seen God. The Israelites believed that no human being could look upon the uncovered glory of God and live. Manoah's dread temporarily swallowed up the hope he had felt earlier.

Manoah's wife encouraged him with sound, faith-filled reasoning. She pointed out that if God intended to kill them, He would not have accepted their sacrifices or given them such wonderful promises about a child. Believers can take comfort knowing that God's past mercies show His loving desire to save and bless them.

The woman gave birth to a baby boy just as God had promised, and she named him Samson, which likely means 'little sun.' As the boy grew, the Lord blessed him with great physical strength and health. God proved faithful to His word, showing that His promises always come to pass.

As Samson grew into a young man, the Holy Spirit began to stir him with supernatural courage and power in the camp of Dan. These spiritual impulses moved him while he lived near his parents' home between Zorah and Eshtaol. God's Spirit was actively preparing him to fulfill his calling and strike against the Philistine oppressors.
